neither one is living. So here is what we're going to do together. First, the shopping list from the back of my little book, the one that feeds one woman for two weeks. A family pack of bone and chicken thighs, two pounds of ground beef, four pork chops, smoked sausage, a bag of frozen salmon filets, a ham steak, 18 eggs, milk, butter, and a block of cheddar. egg noodles, elbow macaroni, rice and quick oats, canned tomatoes, beans, cream of mushroom soup and broth. That comes to about $85 for the two weeks at my grocery store this fall. You need a quarter sheet pan, nine by 13 inches, a small loaf pan, about eight by four, two small baking dishes, the two cup size, a muffin tin, heavy foil and a small slow cooker, one and a half or two quarts because a big one burns small amounts. It's on page seven of my little book. Chicken thigh and little potatoes, one pan. It's the one I made the week after Harold's funeral. Crisp skin, soft potatoes, and everything goes on one pan, so you only wash one pan. It takes about 40 minutes and it makes one plate. Here's what you need. One bone -in chicken thigh, five or six baby potatoes, halved, half a small onion, cut in wedges, one tablespoon of oil, salt and pepper, a quarter teaspoon of paprika, and a quarter teaspoon of garlic powder. Step one, heat the oven to 425 degrees and line the pan with foil. The foil is why there's nothing to scrub later. Honey, that's the best part of cooking for one. Here's my trick and it's the reason for the whole recipe. Pat the chicken skin dry with a paper towel first. Dry skin is crisp skin.

Wet skin steams and then you're eating a sad chicken and nobody wants that for supper. Step 2. Toss the potatoes and the onion with half the oil, a little salt and pepper and spread them out on the pan. Spread them out. If they're piled up, they steam instead of roasting and you want them golden, not gray. Step 3. Rub the chicken with the rest of the oil and the spices and set it skin side up in the middle of the pan. Skin up so the heat hits the skin the whole time and the fat runs down into the potatoes and makes them taste like the chicken. Step 4. Bake at 35 to 40 minutes until the skin is crisp and the potatoes are golden at the edges. Then sit down. Don't stand over the oven. Sit at your table with the good plate. Now the part I won't skip honey. Chicken is done at 165 degrees at the thickest part right next to the bone.

Looks can fool you, so go by the number, not by the color. That's the whole supper, and it's on page seven of my little book, Supper for One. The link to it is right under this video. Every supper in that book is made for one person, and each one tells you what it costs to make. Now the mistake I see most, the one I made for a whole year, you buy a big package and you cook it all at once for two, out of habit. Then half of it goes in the trash on Thursday. Nothing goes in the trash in my kitchen. Cook one, freeze one, or freeze the extra the same day you cook it. When the casseroles came to my door that first week after the funeral, I had more food than a person could eat in a month. 12 dishes, honey. I put half of them in the freezer, in flat bags, with masking tape and a marker, and I wrote the day on every one. That's where this whole system came from.

It came from a grief and a freezer full of other people's kindness. And label every bag. Write what it is and the date. A bag with no name is a bag you'll throw away, I promise you, because three weeks from now, you won't know what's inside. Write it on the bag before it goes in the freezer, not after. Now the freezer plan. It's on page 51 and it's four Sundays. Week one, muffin tin meatloaves and a bean and ham soup, which gives you 12 meatloaves and four bowls of soup. Week two, salsa chicken and egg cups, three bags of chicken and 12 breakfasts. Week three, pulled pork and chicken noodle soup, four sandwiches and three soups. Week four, two little casseroles, one baked and one frozen and a pot of chili, four plates and three chilies. Salsa chicken is my favorite of the lot. Two boneless chicken thighs go in the slow cooker with half a cup of jarred salsa.

Cook it on low for four hours. Don't lift the lid while it cooks because you'll lose the heat. Then shred it with two forks, stir in a quarter cup of cheese, and freeze it in three bags. Tacos, a rice bowl, or a baked potato topping. Chicken to 165 degrees, same as always. The pulled pork is a one pound piece of pork shoulder with half an onion and half a cup of barbecue sauce. The onion goes in the bottom. Then the pork, then the sauce. Cook it on low for seven hours and shred it with forks right in the pot. Freeze it in sandwich sized bags and thaw one in the refrigerator for supper. Four sandwiches out of one small piece of pork and I have never once had to throw one away. The soup I make most is bean and ham soup. Soak a cup of dried navy beans overnight, then drain them.

Put them in a pot with a ham bone or a cup of diced ham, six cups of water, a carrot, a celery stalk, and half an onion, chopped. Simmer it covered for about two hours until the beans are soft. Take out the bone and the bay leaf, pull off any meat and put it back in. Mash some beans against the side of the pot to thicken it and salt at the very end because the ham bone is salty already. When you reheat soup from the freezer, bring it all the way to a boil. I say it every time because it's the right way. Freeze it in flat bags, one bowl each, and lay the bags flat in the freezer so they stack like books on a shelf. Soup freezes fine and it's better the next day anyway. Egg cups are the breakfast that lasts two weeks. Ten eggs, half a cup of milk, a cup of chopped ham or sausage or vegetables, half a cup of shredded cheese, salt and pepper. Grease the muffin tin well.

Divide the meat into the cups. Pour the beaten eggs over and bake at 350 for 20 to 22 minutes until the eggs are set all the way through. Cool them, freeze them, and microwave one from frozen for 45 seconds. Put it on a toasted English muffin and your breakfast is done. 12 little meat loaves are the same trick in a muffin tin. Two pounds of ground beef, one cup of quick oats, two eggs, half a cup of milk, half an onion chopped fine, salt and pepper. Cool them, freeze them in a bag, and take out two at a time. Reheat two in the microwave for about two minutes.

When the family comes home I cook for the whole crowd the way I did in the church basement and then I freeze what's left for myself. Toss the green beans with half the oil, salt and pepper on the lined pan and roast them five minutes then push them aside. Add the salmon, brush it with oil, season it with salt, pepper and a little dill and roast 12 to 15 minutes more. The salmon is done when it flakes apart with a fork at the thickest part.

Fold the foil over and crimp the edges twice so the steam stays in and does the cooking for you. Bake it 25 minutes at 400 degrees and then open it carefully. The pork chop with apples and onions is the fall supper of every farm kitchen I ever knew made small. One boneless pork chop, about 3 quarters of an inch thick, one apple cut in wedges, half an onion sliced, a teaspoon of brown sugar, a tablespoon of melted butter and a pinch of cinnamon.

Toss the apples and the onion with the butter, the brown sugar and the cinnamon right on the lined pan. Salt and pepper the chop, set it on top, and bake at 400 degrees for 20 to 25 minutes. Pork chops are done at 145 degrees, and then they rest three minutes. At the end, spoon the apple juices from the pan over the chop, and it's as good as a restaurant, and you didn't have to tip anybody. The meatballs are my potluck trick. Five frozen cooked meatballs from the big bag, and two carrots cut in sticks. Toss the carrots with a teaspoon of melted butter, a teaspoon of honey, and a pinch of salt. Put the meatballs next to them, and bake 20 minutes at 400 degrees. Then brush the meatballs with the sauce, and bake five more minutes. The sauce can be barbecue sauce, or grape jelly mixed with chili sauce.

Grape jelly and chili sauce is the church potluck meatball sauce and nobody ever guesses what it is. Heat the meatballs until they're hot all the way through. A handful of frozen shrimp and one ear of corn make a summer supper even in the middle of February. Thaw the shrimp in a bowl of cold water for about 10 minutes. Roast the potatoes and the corn with half the melted butter for 15 minutes at 425 degrees. Then add the shrimp, the rest of the butter and the seasoning and roast six to eight minutes until the shrimp turn pink and curl up. Don't overcook them honey. A shrimp that's overdone is like a rubber band and nobody wants to chew on one. Lemon over everything. Turkey burger and fries is burger night for one without the frying pan. Here's the trick.

Soak the potato wedges in cold water for 10 minutes and then dry them well before the oil goes on. They come out crisper that way. Toss the wedges with oil, salt, pepper, and paprika and bake them 15 minutes at 425 degrees. Then add the patty to the pan and bake 15 to 18 minutes more, turning it once. Turkey is done at 165 degrees and beef at 160. Toast the bun on the pan the last two minutes. The loaf pan meatloaf is the church supper meatloaf made with about a quarter of the meat, half a pound of ground beef, a quarter cup of quick oats or crumbs, one egg yolk, two tablespoons of milk, two tablespoons of chopped onion, salt, and pepper. Mix it with your hands just until it holds together and press it into the small loaf pan.

Spread the topping over it, two tablespoons of ketchup, a teaspoon of brown sugar, and half a teaspoon of mustard. Bake it at 350 for 35 to 40 minutes. Beef is done at 160 degrees in the middle. Then let it rest 10 minutes before you slice it. And honey, the cold meatloaf sandwich tomorrow is half the reason to make it. Foil packets mean no dishes at all, and that's my favorite kind of supper. Use heavy foil, about 14 inches long, and fold the edges twice so the steam stays where it belongs. The steam is hotter than you think, and that's the only thing in this whole recipe that can hurt you. And the little pumpkin pies are for the holidays, but I make them any time of year.

One refrigerated pie crust. Cut six circles with a wide glass and press them into the muffin tin. Whisk a cup of canned pumpkin, a third of a cup of sugar, an egg, a half cup of evaporated milk, a teaspoon of pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of salt and fill the cups. Bake at 375 for 25 to 30 minutes until the centers are just set. Keep the pies in the refrigerator.
